_what: What one run of the Namespace tool reads once (src/serve/settings.rs). `account` is the name the person's files are kept under in the rows. `store` says where the person's rows are kept: `{"sqlite": {"file": NAME}}` is a SQLite file of that name in the state folder (the first run makes it; it is for a person's own computer and for tests), `{"run": {"tool": ID, "fd": N}}` is the rows a session of another tool keeps (the shipped file: tool:your-files-names, `live-namespace rows`, the one run that holds the database login), reached by calls through this run's door on descriptor N (the row's invoke.records.fd), so this run holds the byte store's key alone: the engine lets one process reach only hosts every value it holds may go to (src/store/by_calls.rs); `{"postgres": {"connection": NAME}}` is the person's own Postgres database opened by this run itself, `NAME` the held name (`<service>-<field>`) of the attached field that holds its connection string (`own-rows-postgres-connection`: service `own-rows-postgres`, field `connection`), the credential the person's run-sql tool reaches the same database with, by its address (in a run the engine keeps in its sandbox, through the run's proxy: src/store/through_the_run_proxy.rs); a person on one computer with no database sets `store` to a SQLite file instead (`{"sqlite": {"file": NAME}}`, and drops the descriptor-8 field). `call_seconds` is how long one call may take before it answers where it stopped (a paged call resumes there), and how long list_changes `wait` holds: 110, under the engine's own 120 s call deadline (tool-runs.json `deadline_ms`). A write makes about a dozen dependent calls of the names, each at least one round trip to the person's database wherever it is (209 ms from the Mac to the person's own server on Nov 19 2026, so about 4 s of a write is that distance alone), and one share_file of many files still costs about 0.2 to 0.4 s per file from that distance (Nov 20 2026: 20 items with a play and a poster form each took 26 s), so at 30 a share of 65 such items was refused (namespace_source_unavailable) while its files were still being read. `share` (optional) is how a file is shared: `origin` is the https address a share opens at (`<origin>/share/<id>/<key>`, served by the byte route `share_bytes`); without it share_file is refused. `key_prefix` is the folder in the byte store that every file's key starts in; it ends with a slash or is empty. The byte store itself is the person's own `files-store` connection, never a value written here: the engine attaches each field of a connection to the run on a file descriptor (`attached`: the connection, the field and the descriptor, as the tool row's credential_mounts name them), and the run reads each once. Its `endpoint`, `bucket`, `region` and `key-id` make the origin record a first run keeps (src/account_files/bind.rs `make_new`); its `secret` signs the requests and never leaves the run. The state folder is not here: the run is started with the person's own folder (`--state`), where the run keeps its own working files.

share_bytes._what: The public byte route of a share (`serve-shares`, src/share_bytes): `listen` is the loopback address it answers on (a front door's route for /share/* reaches it); `window_bytes` the most one read of the store answers a body with (a body is read a window at a time, so memory holds one window); `recheck_seconds` how often a long body reads the person's share again, so a share stopped mid-play ends the body; `inline_types` the media types shown in the browser (a whole type, or a prefix ending in a slash), every other is offered as a download (a page shows under a sandbox that runs no script); `types_by_ending` the media type of a file whose stored type says nothing (none, or application/octet-stream), by the ending of its name; `page` (absent here, named per computer) the absolute path of the share's page folder: `page.html` and `items.json` filled from the share row and the person's look (settings `site`), and `assets/` answered at /share/assets/<file> (on-a-computer/share-page is the shipped folder). A browser that opens a share gets its page; anything else gets the bytes.
